title: Post-Course Portfolio: Capstone Deployment Exercise
descriptionMarkdown:
# Capstone Deployment Exercise

## Position in the curriculum

This is the closing entry in the post-course portfolio catalog, meant to be done last, applied to a project you have already built rather than a new domain. Its skills (Docker, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, deployment) are exactly the operational skills the final capstone and Phase 5 already required you to demonstrate — this exercise deliberately does not invent a new nineteenth domain to avoid duplicating that content; it asks you to apply it a second time, end to end, to a project of your own choosing.

## What is graded, and what is external

This project has a dedicated, automatically-graded checkpoint: **`rollback-target-checkpoint`** ("Rollback target selector"), a pure in-memory `RollbackSelector.run(String input)` program implementing exactly the decision of which prior version to roll back to given a deployment history. Passing its hidden tests proves your rollback-selection logic is correct, independent of any real Docker build or health-check wiring.

Actually building the container image, running Compose against a real PostgreSQL instance, and demonstrating a live readiness probe and graceful shutdown are external and self-reviewed — this checkpoint only proves the decision logic your runbook depends on.

## Architecture overview

```text
Dockerfile (multi-stage)         <- build stage (JDK) -> small non-root runtime image (JRE)
docker-compose.yml                <- your chosen application + a real postgres service, env-supplied config
/actuator/health/readiness        <- reports not-ready before the database is reachable or during shutdown
ROLLBACK.md                       <- your checkpoint's selection rule, applied as an operational runbook
```

## Build it as vertical slices

1. **Slice 1 — port the checkpoint logic into your runbook.** Your `RollbackSelector` rule (skip back past the most recent deployment to the nearest earlier healthy one) becomes the exact decision procedure `ROLLBACK.md` documents; a human or a script should be able to follow it mechanically.
2. **Slice 2 — the multi-stage Dockerfile.** A build stage compiles the application; the runtime stage ships only the built artifact and a JRE, running as a non-root user.
3. **Slice 3 — Compose with a real database.** Application and PostgreSQL as separate services; all connection details supplied through environment variables, never baked into the image.
4. **Slice 4 — real readiness and graceful shutdown.** Demonstrate the readiness endpoint reporting not-ready while the database container is stopped, and confirm an in-flight request completes after a termination signal rather than being cut off.
5. **Slice 5 — a rehearsed rollback.** Deploy a deliberately broken version, observe it fail health checks, and follow your own runbook to restore the previous working version.

## Common pitfalls

- **Hard-coding the readiness endpoint to always return healthy.** It must reflect a genuinely checked dependency (the database connection), exactly as the checkpoint's own rollback logic assumes deployments are marked healthy or unhealthy based on a real signal.
- **Baking database credentials or a hostname into the image.** Supply every environment-specific value through Compose's environment configuration.
- **Treating the most recent deployment as the rollback target even when it is the one that just failed.** The checkpoint's own contract explicitly skips the last entry and looks strictly before it — apply that same rule in your runbook.
- **Never actually rehearsing the rollback.** A runbook nobody has followed end to end is a guess, not a verified procedure.

## How to self-test what the checkpoint cannot reach

- Run `docker compose up` from a clean checkout on a machine that has never seen the project and confirm it comes up against a fresh database with migrations applied.
- Stop the database container mid-run and confirm the readiness endpoint reports not-ready, then restart it and confirm readiness recovers.
- Send the application container a termination signal during an in-flight request and confirm that request completes before the process exits.

## Required evidence

- A `docker compose up` from a clean checkout that brings up the application and a fresh PostgreSQL instance, runs pending migrations automatically, and serves traffic, with the exact commands documented in a README.
- Evidence the container image runs as a non-root user (a `docker inspect` or `whoami` check inside the running container).
- A demonstration of the readiness endpoint returning not-ready while the database container is deliberately stopped, and ready again once it is restored.
- A demonstration of graceful shutdown: sending the container a termination signal while a request is in flight, and confirming that request completes before the process exits, per the interruption/cancellation discipline from the concurrency chapter.
- A one-page rollback runbook: exact commands to revert to the previous image tag and confirm the rollback succeeded, following your checkpoint's own target-selection rule.

## Review and completion

A reviewer runs your `docker compose up` command on a machine that has never seen this project before, confirms the application comes up correctly against a fresh database with migrations already applied, stops the database container mid-run to confirm the readiness probe reacts correctly, then sends a shutdown signal during an in-flight request and confirms it completes rather than being cut off.
learningObjectives: Complete the graded rollback target selector checkpoint and apply its verified selection rule as a real operational runbook
Build a small, non-root, multi-stage container image for an application built earlier in this course
Run an application and a real database together via Docker Compose with externally supplied configuration
Demonstrate a readiness probe correctly reflecting a genuinely unhealthy dependency, not just a hard-coded true
Demonstrate graceful shutdown completing an in-flight request rather than dropping it
